lessons.culture: In Egypt people often answer "where do you live?" with the area, such as مدينة نصر or المعادي, rather than a full address, and a flat is usually in a building called عمارة. lessons.culture: In Egypt floors are counted up from the الدور الأرضي (ground floor), so الدور الأول is the one above it, and many families live in a flat (شقة) in a building. The roof (السطح) is a real part of the home, used for washing lines and for sitting out on summer evenings. When you praise someone's home you say ما شاء الله, and the owner answers تسلم or ربنا يبارك لك.

dialogue.speaker: Heba

response.english: At the end of the corridor.

lessons.culture: In Egypt, الحمام is the everyday way to ask for the toilet as well as the bathroom, and asking فين الحمام؟ is perfectly polite. A flat has a صالة (hall) in the middle, and the صالون is the best room, kept tidy for guests, while the family sits in أوضة القعاد. Visitors are shown the house with the phrase اتفضل.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "bathroom"?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: الحمام is the bathroom and also the toilet.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "The bedrooms are upstairs"?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: فوق is "up" or "upstairs"; تحت is "downstairs".

exercises.prompt: Which phrase asks "Where are the stairs?"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: سلم is the stairs; the question word فين comes at the end.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "المطبخ _____؟" Meaning: Where is the kitchen?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; Cairenes say فين.

exercises.tip: فين is "where".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "الباب _____." Meaning: The door is closed.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; Cairenes say مقفول.

exercises.tip: مقفول is locked or closed.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "الحمام فين؟" Say it is at the end of the corridor.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: آخر is "the end of"; طرقة is the corridor.

exercises.prompt: A guest asks you: "أوضة الضيوف جاهزة؟" Say yes, it is ready.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: جاهزة has ة because أوضة is feminine.

exercises.prompt: Say in Egyptian Arabic: "This is my bedroom."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: دي is "this" for a feminine thing; أوضة is a room.

exercises.prompt: Say in Egyptian Arabic: "Let us go up to the roof."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: طلع means to go up.

exercises.prompt: Say in Egyptian Arabic: "The balcony is next to the bedroom."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: البلكونة is the balcony; جنب is "next to".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "جنب / البلكونة / أوضة النوم"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: Say the thing first, then جنب and the place.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "نطلع / يلا / السطح"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: يلا starts a suggestion.

dialogue.speaker: Khaled
dialogue.english: Thank you, Mostafa.

dialogue.english: It is a bit hot.

dialogue.speaker: Mostafa
dialogue.english: If you want anything, tell me.

lessons.culture: In Egypt people say ولّع النور (literally "light the light") and طفّي النور for the light, and شغّل for a fan or a television. A machine that has broken down is often called بايظة (spoiled) as well as مش شغالة. A guest in a home is usually offered a blanket and a pillow without asking, and a host says لو عايز حاجة قولّي (if you want anything, tell me).

exercises.prompt: Which word means "mirror"?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; Cairenes say مراية.

exercises.tip: مراية is the everyday word.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase asks "Where is the key?"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: مفتاح is a key; فين is "where".

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "Open the window" (to a man)?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; Cairenes say شباك.

exercises.tip: شباك is the everyday word for window; to a woman say افتحي.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ المروحة." Meaning: Switch on the fan. (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: شغّل is used for a fan, a television or a machine.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "الغسالة مش _____." Meaning: The washing machine does not work.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: مش makes it negative; شغالة is "working".

exercises.prompt: Your host says: "الجو حر. شغّل المروحة." Say right away.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: حاضر is the everyday "right away".

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "الريموت فين؟" Say it is on the sofa.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: على is "on"; كنبة is a sofa.

exercises.prompt: Say in Egyptian Arabic: "I need a blanket." (male speaker)

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: A woman says محتاجة.

exercises.prompt: Say in Egyptian Arabic: "Switch off the light." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: طفّى means to switch off; to a woman say طفّي too.

exercises.prompt: Say in Egyptian Arabic: "There is a bed in the room."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: فيه means "there is".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "جنب / المراية / الباب"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: Say the thing first, then جنب and the place.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "في / سرير / الأوضة / فيه"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic (or a bookish word); everyday Cairene speech says it differently.

exercises.tip: فيه comes first and means "there is".

challenge.title: Meeting Family Over a Meal
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Egyptian conversation of at least 10 lines. It must ask about someone's family, name at least one relative, say you are hungry or thirsty, order food or a drink, use the fixed exchange بالهنا والشفا / الله يعافيك, and ask for the bill. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 2 and address both a man and a woman.
required_elements: A question about family using كام فرد في عيلتك؟ or عندك إخوات؟
A relative named with أمي, أبويا, أخويا, أختي, جوزي, مراتي, ابني or بنتي.
A statement of hunger or thirst using جعان, جعانة or عطشان.
An order using عايز آكل or عايز أشرب.
The fixed exchange بالهنا والشفا / الله يعافيك.
A request for the bill using الحساب لو سمحت or الحساب كام؟
Both a masculine form (إنت متجوز؟) and a feminine form (إنتي متجوزة؟).

dialogue.speaker: Sameh
dialogue.english: How are you, Dina?

dialogue.speaker: Dina
dialogue.english: Thank God, how are you, Sameh?

dialogue.speaker: Sameh
dialogue.english: Fine. Are you married?

dialogue.speaker: Dina
dialogue.transliteration: aywa, we 3andi bint. we enta metgawwez?
dialogue.english: Yes, and I have a daughter. And you, are you married?

dialogue.speaker: Sameh
dialogue.arabic: لا، لسه أعزب. كام فرد في عيلتك؟
dialogue.transliteration: la2, lissa a3zab. kaam fard fi 3eltak?
dialogue.english: No, still single. How many are in your family?

dialogue.speaker: Dina
dialogue.arabic: إحنا خمسة. أنا جعانة، إنت جعان؟
dialogue.transliteration: e7na khamsa. ana ga3aana, enta ga3aan?
dialogue.english: We are five. I'm hungry, are you?

dialogue.speaker: Sameh
dialogue.arabic: أيوه، عايز آكل طعمية وأشرب شاي.
dialogue.transliteration: aywa, 3ayez aakol ta3meyya we ashrab shaay.
dialogue.english: Yes, I want to eat falafel and drink tea.

dialogue.speaker: Dina
dialogue.english: And I want coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Sameh
dialogue.english: Enjoy your meal.

dialogue.speaker: Dina
dialogue.english: May God give you health.

dialogue.speaker: Sameh
dialogue.english: The bill, please.
